transcript.content: Hello, I’m Dr. —. What brings you in today?

Well, Dr. —, it’s... it’s a whole mess of things, really. To be honest with you, I just keep forgetting things that I really, really shouldn’t be forgetting. And I don't mean just misplacing my reading glasses or the newspaper, though Lord knows I do that enough. I mean important stuff. 

Like my heart follow-up appointments. I had this whole thing with my ticker a while back, and they tell me to come in for a check-up, and I swear I mean to go, but the day just comes and goes and I completely miss it. Or I'll get a message from the nurse, and I just never get around to calling the clinic back. I'll listen to the voicemail, I'll tell myself, 'call them right now before you forget,' and then I walk into the kitchen to get a glass of water and poof, the thought is completely gone from my brain. 

And it’s not just the medical stuff, either. It’s everyday things, things I’ve done my whole life. I’ll head over to a buddy's house or start on a project—I like to stay busy, you know, doing handy work and tinkering around since I stopped working—and I’ll show up for a repair job and realize I didn't even bring the right tools. I'll drive all the way over there, get out of the truck, ready to work, and realize my toolbox is still sitting right on the workbench in the garage where I left it. It’s just driving me crazy, you know? You're standing in a driveway looking like a fool because you can't keep your ducks in a row for five minutes. So, I guess that's what brought me in. I just can't keep dropping the ball on things like this.
Have you always had this kind of trouble with forgetfulness and distractibility, even back when you were a child?

Oh, boy. Yeah. If you asked my older sister, she’d probably just laugh and say I haven't changed a bit since 1965. It’s funny you ask about when I was a kid, because... well, back then, they didn't really know what to do with a kid like me. 

I went to this little Catholic grade school, and I swear, I must have driven those poor nuns half to death. Even as a boy in grade school, I was the kid who just absolutely could not stay in his seat. I mean, my legs would just be bouncing under the desk, and I'd be up at the pencil sharpener for the fifth time, or standing up to look out the window at a passing truck, or leaning over to bother whoever was unlucky enough to sit next to me. 

And I was always blurting out the answers before the teacher even finished asking the question. It was like... I knew the answer, or at least I thought I did, and I just couldn't hold it in, you know? It just flew right out of my mouth before I could even think to raise my hand. My mother, God rest her soul, she used to dread checking my pockets or my bookbag when I got home because there was always—and I mean always—a note sent home from the teacher about me talking too much. She'd sit me down at the kitchen table, smoothing out this crumpled piece of paper, and ask, 'Why can't you just sit still and be quiet like the other boys?' And I never had a good answer for her. I just had this... this motor running inside me all the time. My dad would get home from the plant, and he'd have to sign the note, and then there'd be a whole big lecture about discipline and listening, but the very next day, I'd be right back to jumping out of my chair and running my mouth. So, yeah, it's been a lifelong thing, just constantly going and going and talking out of turn...
